lesson.title: Climbing the Graph: What Increasing Really Means
lesson.summary: A function is increasing on an interval when its output values rise as the input moves to the right, and the First Derivative Test turns that visual idea into a precise algebraic check: f is increasing wherever f prime is positive.
lesson.body:
A function f is increasing on an interval I if, for every pair of numbers a and b in I with a less than b, it is also true that f(a) is less than f(b). In plain language, as you trace the graph from left to right within that interval, the curve only goes uphill, never flat and never downhill. This is a statement about the whole interval, not about a single point, so "increasing at a point" is really shorthand for "increasing on some small interval around that point."

The derivative gives a fast way to check this without plotting every pair of points. If f is differentiable on an interval and f'(x) is greater than 0 for every x in that interval, then f is increasing there. The reasoning rests on the Mean Value Theorem: for any a less than b in the interval, there is some c between them with f'(c) equal to the slope, f(b) minus f(a), divided by b minus a. If f' is positive everywhere on the interval, that slope must be positive too, which forces f(b) to be greater than f(a). This is exactly the logic behind the First Derivative Test: the sign of f' on either side of a critical number tells you which way the graph is heading.

Consider f(x) = x^3 - 3x^2 - 9x + 5. To find where f is increasing, first differentiate: f'(x) = 3x^2 - 6x - 9. Factor out a 3 and factor the quadratic: f'(x) = 3(x^2 - 2x - 3) = 3(x - 3)(x + 1). Setting f'(x) = 0 gives critical numbers x = -1 and x = 3, which split the real line into three intervals: (negative infinity, -1), (-1, 3), and (3, positive infinity).

Test one point from each interval in the factored form 3(x - 3)(x + 1). At x = -2: 3(-2 - 3)(-2 + 1) = 3(-5)(-1) = 15, which is positive. At x = 0: 3(0 - 3)(0 + 1) = 3(-3)(1) = -9, which is negative. At x = 4: 3(4 - 3)(4 + 1) = 3(1)(5) = 15, which is positive. So f' is positive on (negative infinity, -1), negative on (-1, 3), and positive again on (3, positive infinity).

Since f' is greater than 0 exactly on (negative infinity, -1) and (3, positive infinity), f is increasing on those two intervals. Many texts write these as the closed intervals (negative infinity, -1] and [3, positive infinity) instead, tucking the critical number itself into the increasing interval, since f is still continuous there and the inequality f(a) less than f(b) still holds for every pair of points you pick from the closed interval, the derivative just happens to touch zero at that one boundary point. Either notation is acceptable as long as it is used consistently. This same cubic will come back throughout the chapters on decreasing functions, concavity, and inflection points, since one worked example that keeps reappearing is easier to hold in memory than a dozen unrelated ones.
